title: Derivative of an averaged Gaussian indicator
statement: Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be measurable, and let $u\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\sin u\ne0$. For $x\in\mathbb R^n$, define $F(x)=\int 1_A(\cos u\,x+\sin u\,y)\,d\gamma_n(y)$, where $\gamma_n$ is standard Gaussian measure. The function $F$ is differentiable at every $x$, and its derivative is the linear functional obtained by composing multiplication by $\cos u$ with the integral, over $z\in\mathbb R^n$ with respect to Lebesgue measure, of $1_A(z)$ times the derivative in the mean vector $c$ of the product Gaussian density $\prod_{i=1}^n p_{\sin^2u}(c_i,z_i)$, evaluated at $c=\cos u\,x$.
replaced: Let $\gamma_n$ be standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^n$. For $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $\theta\in\mathbb R$, put $u_\theta(x)=\int1_A(\cos\theta\,x+\sin\theta\,y)\,d\gamma_n(y)$. If $A$ is measurable and $\sin u\ne0$, $u_u$ is differentiable at every $x\in\mathbb R^n$, with $D u_u(x)[h]=\cos u\int1_A(z)\,\partial_c[\prod_i p_{\sin^2u}(c_i,z_i)]_{c=\cos u\,x}[h]\,dz$, where $p_v$ is the Gaussian density and $\partial_c$ is differentiation in the mean vector.
